newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican prosecutors grill Salinas anew over murder.
newsitem.headline: Mexican prosecutors grill Salinas anew over murder.

text.p: Prosecutors investigating the 1994 murder of a top politician interrogated former Mexican president Carlos Salinas for more than 16 hours about the crime, the Attorney-General's office said on Tuesday.
Two senior prosecutors travelled to Dublin, Ireland, where Salinas lives in self-imposed exile, and questioned him on Monday, the office said in a statement.

Salinas ruled Mexico from 1988 to 1994 but fled the country in March 1995, shortly after his brother Raul was arrested on charges of masterminding the murder of their former brother-in-law, ruling party secretary-general Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu.

Raul Salinas remains in a maximum-security jail awaiting trial on the charges of arranging the assassination of Ruiz Massieu outside a Mexico City hotel in September 1994. At the time of his death, Ruiz Massieu was divorced from Raul and Carlos Salinas's sister Adriana.
The Attorney-General's office gave no details of the interrogation beyond saying that Salinas had answered 216 questions at the Mexican embassy in Dublin.
Spokesmen refused to give additional information or to say whether Salinas would face further questioning.

Monday's session was the second round of interrogation Salinas has faced. Last November, he was questioned in Ireland for about 12 hours about a different assassination, the 1994 murder of ruling party presidential candidate Luis Donaldo Colosio.
Salinas said after that interrogation that he had no knowledge about any plot to kill Colosio, whom he described as a dear friend and a much-missed ally.

Opinion polls published here last year showed a majority of Mexicans believed Salinas had some knowledge of, or involvement with, Colosio's death but the former president has always vigorously denied this.
While in office Salinas was hugely popular but his reputation crashed when the Mexican peso collapsed without warning only weeks after he left office, plunging the country into a deep recession.
